source.title: Exploring Progressions: A Collection of Problems

accepted.question_text: Let (a_n)_{n\ge 1} be an arithmetic progression and let c be a fixed real constant. Prove that the scaled sequence (c a_n)_{n\ge 1} is also an arithmetic progression.

evidence.quote: Show that if the sequence a1, a2, . . . , an, . . . , is an arithmetic progression, so is the sequence c · a1, c · a2, . . . , c · an, . . . , where c is a constant.

accepted.question_text: Determine every possible common difference d of an arithmetic progression whose first term is a1 = 6 and which has both 62 and 104 among its terms.

evidence.quote: Determine the difference of each arithmetic progression which has first term a1 = 6 and contains the numbers 62 and 104 as its terms.

accepted.question_text: Prove that the three irrational numbers √2, √3, and √5 cannot all occur as terms of a single arithmetic progression.

evidence.quote: Show that the irrational numbers √2, √3, √5 cannot be terms of an arithmetic progression.

accepted.question_text: Let (a_n) be an arithmetic progression. Suppose ak = α, am = β, and aℓ = γ for natural numbers k, m, and ℓ. Prove that the indices and values satisfy α(m − ℓ) + β(ℓ − k) + γ(k − m) = 0.
accepted.context_brief: Linear relation among indexed AP terms

evidence.quote: If a1, a2, . . . , an, . . . is an arithmetic progression and ak = α, am = β, aℓ = γ, show that the natural numbers k, m, ℓ and the real numbers α, β, γ, must satisfy the condition α · (m − ℓ) + β · (ℓ − k) + γ · (k − m) = 0.

accepted.question_text: Assume α, β, and γ are three successive terms of an arithmetic progression. Prove that the three numbers α²(β + γ), β²(γ + α), and γ²(α + β) are also successive terms of an arithmetic progression.

evidence.quote: If the numbers α, β, γ are successive terms of an arithmetic progression, then the same holds true for the numbers α2 ·(β + γ), β2 ·(γ + α), γ2 · (α + β).

accepted.question_text: For each natural number k, let Sk denote the sum of the first k terms of the arithmetic progression whose first term is k and whose common difference is d = 2k − 1. Find a closed form for S1 + S2 + ··· + Sk.

evidence.quote: If Sk denotes the sum of the first k terms of the arithmetic progression with first term k and difference d = 2k−1, find the sum S1+S2+. . .+Sk.

accepted.question_text: Partition the odd positive integers into blocks {1}, {3, 5}, {7, 9, 11}, …, so that the nth block consists of n consecutive odd integers and begins at n(n − 1) + 1. Determine the sum of the numbers in the nth block.

evidence.quote: We divide the odd natural numbers into groups or classes as follows: {1}, {3, 5}, {7, 9, 11}, . . . ; the nth group contains n odd numbers starting with (n ·(n − 1) + 1) (verify this). Find the sum of the members of the nth group.

accepted.question_text: Partition the even positive integers into blocks {2}, {4, 6}, {8, 10, 12}, …, so that the nth block consists of n consecutive even integers and begins at n(n − 1) + 2. Determine the sum of the numbers in the nth block.

evidence.quote: We divide the even natural numbers into groups as follows: {2}, {4, 6}, {8, 10, 12}, . . . ; the nth group contains n even numbers starting with (n(n − 1) + 2). Find the ’sum of the members of the nth group.

accepted.question_text: Let n1 < n2 < ··· < nk be natural numbers, and let (a_n) be an arithmetic progression such that the selected terms a_{n1}, a_{n2}, …, a_{nk} themselves form an arithmetic progression. Prove that each ratio (a_{nk} − a_{ni}) / (a_{n2} − a_{n1}) for i = 1, 2, …, k − 1 is a rational number; explicitly, this includes (a_{nk} − a_{n1})/(a_{n2} − a_{n1}), (a_{nk} − a_{n2})/(a_{n2} − a_{n1}), …, and (a_{nk} − a_{n,k−1})/(a_{n2} − a_{n1}).
accepted.context_brief: Rational ratios from sampled AP terms

evidence.quote: Let n1, n2, . . . , nk be k natural numbers such that n1 < n2 < . . . < nk; if the real numbers, an1, an2, . . . , ank, are members of an arithmetic progression ... show that the real numbers: ank − an1 / an2 − an1, ank − an2 / an2 − an1, . . . , ank − ank−1 / an2 − an1, are all rational numbers.

accepted.question_text: Let m and n be natural numbers, and let (a_k) be an arithmetic progression with am = 1/n and an = 1/m. Prove all of the following: (a) the first term equals the common difference, a1 = d; (b) for every natural number t, the term a_{t mn} equals t; and (c) if S_{t mn} denotes the sum of the first tmn terms, then S_{t mn} = ((mn + 1)/2) t.

evidence.quote: Let m and n be natural numbers. If in an arithmetic progression a1, a2, . . . , ak, . . .; the term am is equal to 1/n ... and the term an is equal to 1/m ... prove the following three statements. (a) The first term a1 is equal to the difference d. (b) If t is any natural number, then at·(mn) = t ... (c) If St·(mn) ... then St·(mn) = 1/2 ·(mn + 1)·t.

accepted.question_text: Let a, b, and c be distinct real numbers that are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove both identities: (a) 2/b = 1/(b − a) + 1/(b − c), and (b) (b + a)/(b − a) + (b + c)/(b − c) = 2.

evidence.quote: If the distinct real numbers a, b, c are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression show that (a) 2/b = 1/(b−a) + 1/(b−c) and (b) b+a /(b−a) + b+c /(b−c) = 2

accepted.question_text: Let α, β, and γ be distinct real numbers that are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that α, α − γ, and α − β are also consecutive terms of a harmonic progression.

evidence.quote: If the distinct reals α, β, γ are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression then the same is true for the numbers α, α − γ, α − β.

accepted.question_text: Let (a_n) be a geometric progression, and let k, ℓ, and m be natural numbers. If ak = β, aℓ = γ, and am = δ, prove that β^(ℓ−m) · γ^(m−k) · δ^(k−ℓ) = 1.

evidence.quote: Let a = a1, a2, a3, . . . , an, . . . , be a geometric progression and k, ℓ, m natural numbers. If ak = β, aℓ = γ, am = δ, show that βℓ−m · γm−k · δk−ℓ = 1.

accepted.question_text: Let a1 = a, a2, … be a geometric progression with positive first term a and positive ratio r ≠ 1. Let n and k be natural numbers with n > k + 1. If A is the sum of the first k terms and B is the sum of the last k terms among the first n terms, express the ratio r solely in terms of A and B, and also express the first term a solely in terms of A and B.
accepted.context_brief: Recover GP parameters from partial sums

evidence.quote: Suppose that n and k are natural numbers such that n > k + 1; and a1 = a, a2, . . . , at, . . . a geometric progression, with positive ratio r 6= 1, and positive first term a. If A is the value of the sum of the first k terms of the progression and B is the value of the last k terms among the n first terms, express the ratio r in terms of A and B only; and also the first term a in terms of A and B.

accepted.question_text: Evaluate the infinite series 2/7 + 4/7² + 2/7³ + 4/7⁴ + 2/7⁵ + 4/7⁶ + ···.
Assume α, β, and γ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression, and β, γ, and δ are nonzero consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that α/β = γ/δ.
accepted.context_brief: Link between AP and HP data

evidence.quote: If the numbers α, β, γ are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression and the nonzero numbers β, γ, δ are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression, show that α/β = γ/δ.

accepted.question_text: Let α, β, and γ be positive real numbers in arithmetic progression. Let x be the geometric mean of α and β, and let y be the geometric mean of β and γ. Prove that x², β², and y² are consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression, and provide two explicit numerical examples.

evidence.quote: Suppose that the positive reals α, β, γ are successive terms of an arithmetic progression and let x be the geometric mean of α and β; and let y be the geometric mean of β and γ. Prove that x^2, β^2, y^2 are successive terms of an arithmetic progression. Give two numerical examples.

accepted.question_text: Let a, b, and c be nonzero real numbers that are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression. Prove that the three numbers a − b/2, b/2, and c − b/2 are consecutive terms of a geometric progression, and give two numerical examples.

evidence.quote: Show that if the nonzero real numbers a, b, c are consecutive terms of a harmonic progression, then the numbers a − b/2, b/2, c − b/2, must be consecutive terms of a geometric progression. Give two numerical examples.

accepted.question_text: Compute explicit closed forms for the two finite sums: (i) Σ_{i=1}^n i/2^i, and (ii) 1 + 3/2 + 5/4 + ··· + (2n − 1)/2^(n−1).
accepted.context_brief: Finite sums with powers of two

evidence.quote: Compute the following sums: (i) 1/2 + 2/2^2 + . . . + n/2^n

accepted.question_text: Suppose a sequence (a_n) satisfies the recurrence a_{n+1} = (a_n + λ)ω, where λ and ω are fixed real numbers with ω ≠ 1. Prove by induction that for every natural number n, a_n = a_1 ω^(n−1) + λ((ω^n − ω)/(ω − 1)), and then use that formula to show that the partial sums satisfy S_n = a_1 + a_2 + ··· + a_n = a_1((ω^n − 1)/(ω − 1)) + λ((ω^(n+1) − nω^2 + (n−1)ω)/(ω−1)^2).

evidence.quote: Suppose that the sequence a1, a2, . . . , an, . . . satisfies an+1 = (an+λ)·ω, where λ and ω are fixed real numbers with ω 6= 1. (i) Use mathematical induction to prove that for every natural number, an = a1 · ω^(n−1) + λ · ((ω^n−ω)/(ω−1)). (ii) Use your answer in part (i) to show that, Sn = a1 + a2 + . . . + an = a1 · ((ω^n − 1)/(ω − 1)) + λ · ((ω^(n+1)−n·ω^2+(n−1)ω)/(ω−1)^2).

accepted.question_text: Let am, am+1, …, an be consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression, where the number of terms n − m + 1 is even. Prove that their arithmetic mean equals the average of the two middle terms, namely (a_{(n+m−1)/2} + a_{(n+m+1)/2})/2.

evidence.quote: (ii) If the natural number is even, then the arithmetic mean of the reals am, am+1, . . . , an−1, an must be the average of the two middle terms a((n+m−1)/2) and a((n+m+1)/2).
23. Prove part (ii) of Theorem 4.

accepted.question_text: For a geometric progression with negative first term a and ratio r, work out the full analogue of the case-by-case analysis previously given for positive first term: describe the sign pattern, monotonic behavior, and limiting behavior for the different ranges of r.

evidence.quote: (viii) What happens when the first term a is negative? A similar analysis holds (see Exercise 24).
24. Work out part (viii) of Remark 5.

accepted.question_text: Prove the geometric-progression analogue of Theorem 4. Specifically, let am, am+1, …, an be positive consecutive terms of a geometric progression. Show that if n − m + 1 is odd, then the geometric mean of all these terms equals the middle term a_{(m+n)/2}; and if n − m + 1 is even, then the geometric mean of all these terms equals the geometric mean of the two middle terms a_{(n+m−1)/2} and a_{(n+m+1)/2}.

evidence.quote: 25. Prove the analogue of Theorem 4 for geometric progressions: if the (n − m + 1) positive real numbers am, am+1, . . . , an−1, an are successive terms of a geometric progression, then (i) If the natural number (n−m+1) is odd, then the geometric mean of the (n − m + 1) terms is simply the middle number a((m+n)/2). (ii) If the natural number (n − m + 1) is even, then the geometric mean of the (n− m + 1) terms must be the geometric mean of the two middle terms a((n+m−1)/2) and a((n+m+1)/2).
